title: The Curious Case of Estonian
bodyHtml:
Estonian is a Uralic language closely related to Finnish; it is spoken by over a million people in Estonia. In Estonian, as in many languages around the world, nouns (and adjectives) take different forms (called "cases") according to their role in the sentence. For example, in the sentence below, there are three forms of the word horse. This is similar to the difference between he, him, and his in English.

Hobunenägihobusthobusega.
horse.nominativesawhorse.partitivehorse.comitative

'A horse saw a horse with a horse.'

Estonian nouns have a lot of different forms depending on their case and their number (singular or plural). The table below illustrates various forms for different nouns and adjectives; the exact meaning of these different cases is not relevant to this problem. Be careful, however: exactly four of the forms in the table below are mistakes! Note that õ, ä, ö, and ü are vowels.

questions.promptHtml: The Partitive Singular of 'singer' is printed as laulja. Write the correct form.
questions.partPrompt: Exactly four forms in the big table are mistakes. Write down the correct form of each one.

questions.promptHtml: The Adessive Singular of 'sister' is printed as õdel. Write the correct form.
The Partitive Singular of 'yellow' is printed as kollaset. Write the correct form.
The Genitive Singular of 'big' is printed as suur. Write the correct form.

questions.partPrompt: Fill in the blanks in the second table.

hints.text: Do not think about what the cases mean. Just compare the six Estonian forms in a single row: several of them are one letter longer than another form in the same row.

Four of the columns are predictable from the other two. The Adessive Singular and the Nominative Plural are built from the Genitive Singular by adding one consonant each; the Genitive Plural is built from the Partitive Singular; and the Adessive Plural is the Genitive Plural plus one consonant. A cell is a mistake when it breaks one of these relationships.

Try the 'reason' row, which is not one of the graded items. Genitive Singular põhjuse plus -l gives põhjusel (matches the Adessive Singular) and plus -d gives põhjused (matches the Nominative Plural). Partitive Singular põhjust plus -e gives põhjuste (matches the Genitive Plural), and that plus -l gives põhjustel. Every cell in that row checks out, so the row is clean. Notice that when the Partitive Singular ends in a vowel instead of -t, the Genitive Plural adds -de instead of -e (compare maja and majade).

explanationHtml:
What a "case" is

A case is just a shape a noun takes depending on its job in the sentence. English does a tiny bit of this with pronouns: he (subject), him (object), his (possessor). Estonian does it with every noun and adjective, and there are a lot of shapes. The good news for this problem is that you never need to know what "adessive" or "partitive" mean. You only need to see how the columns relate to each other.

Step 1: find the columns that are just one letter longer

Look at the 'house' row: maja, maja, majal, majad, majade, majadel. The third form is the first plus -l. The fourth is the first plus -d. The sixth is the fifth plus -l. Check 'nest' and the same thing happens: pesa, pesal, pesad, pesade, pesadel.

So the working rules are:

  • Adessive Singular = Genitive Singular + l
  • Nominative Plural = Genitive Singular + d
  • Adessive Plural = Genitive Plural + l

Step 2: connect the Genitive Plural to the Partitive Singular

The Genitive Plural is not based on the Genitive Singular. Compare 'man': Genitive Singular mehe, but Genitive Plural meeste. What it does match is the Partitive Singular meest plus -e. The same works for 'story' (lugu plus -de gives lugude) and 'bean' (uba plus -de gives ubade).

The choice between -e and -de depends on the end of the Partitive Singular: if it ends in t, add -e (valget gives valgete); if it ends in a vowel, add -de (nime gives nimede). Either way, the Genitive Plural tells you the Partitive Singular and vice versa.

Step 3: hunt for the four broken cells

Now scan every row and see whether all four relationships hold.

  • 'singer': Genitive Plural lauljate ends in -te, so the Partitive Singular must end in t: it should be lauljat, not laulja. (Also, lauljatel is lauljate + l, confirming the Genitive Plural is fine.)
  • 'sister': Genitive Singular is õe, and the Nominative Plural õed agrees with it. So the Adessive Singular must be õe + l = õel, not õdel.
  • 'yellow': Genitive Plural kollaste means the Partitive Singular ends in st: kollast, not kollaset. Compare 'big', whose Partitive Singular is suurt and Genitive Plural suurte.
  • 'big': the Adessive Singular suurel and Nominative Plural suured both point to a Genitive Singular suure, so the printed suur is wrong.

That is exactly four mistakes, so you can stop.

Step 4: fill the small table

'moon'. You are given Partitive Singular kuud and Adessive Singular kuul. Strip the -l from the adessive: Genitive Singular is kuu (a). Then Nominative Plural = kuu + d = kuud (b) - it happens to look the same as the partitive, just as with 'ice' and 'road'. Genitive Plural = kuud + e = kuude (c), and Adessive Plural = kuudel (d).

'human'. Genitive Singular inimese gives Adessive Singular inimesel (f) and Nominative Plural inimesed (g). Genitive Plural inimeste ends in -te, so the Partitive Singular is inimest (e), and the Adessive Plural is inimestel (h). This row behaves exactly like 'yellow'.

'fish'. Partitive Singular kala ends in a vowel, and Nominative Plural kalad shows the Genitive Singular is kala (i), just like 'house'. So Adessive Singular kalal (j), Genitive Plural kala + de = kalade (k), Adessive Plural kaladel (l).

The moral

Estonian stems can change unpredictably (õe versus õde, loo versus lugu), but the endings are highly regular, and each irregular stem shows up in a fixed set of columns. Once you know which column each other column is built from, you can both spot errors and generate missing forms without knowing a word of Estonian.
_reviewNotes: All answer keys taken from the official solution page. The booklet does not label the four C1 items, so ids C1.1-C1.4 were assigned in the order the official solution lists them (laulja, õdel, kollaset, suur); each prompt names the exact word and cell so grading stays unambiguous. Points: 5 total split as 0.5 per C1 item (2) and 0.25 per C2 blank (3). No figures in this problem.
